headline: Race at 3.6 Knots: Bass on Wire Line at Valiant, Slack Hits 15:42
subhead: The bunker blitz corridor finally reached the Sound's hardest water, and the albies are close enough to smell — but they're not here yet.
body_markdown:
Race Rock buoy was showing 3.6 knots of ebb at 1 PM Tuesday, and that's the number that told me to load the wire line instead of the topwater bag. Anything under four knots at the Rock and you can still hold bottom with 30 feet of 32-pound Monel and a white bucktail; push past four-and-a-half and you're just along for the ride. Slack at Valiant Rock came right on schedule at 15:42, and that eight-minute window before the current built back the other way produced the two best fish of my week — a 34-inch striper that ate a chartreuse bucktail with a white worm trailer stacked right on the down-current edge of the boulder field in about 42 feet, and a fat 29-incher that came off the same drift ten minutes later on a Ballistic Missile in bunker color.

That's the pattern right now: hunt the slack, not the roar. The Race and Plum Gut have both been running hard on this new moon cycle — we flagged it last week that the building tidal flow into August 12 would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened. The bass haven't left the rips, but they've gotten particular about when they'll eat in them. Full ebb or full flood, you can mark them stacked over the rockpile on the meter and still get refused. Cut the speed down to that four-knot window and they light up the rod tip instead of your sonar screen.

Water's still holding summer temps end to end — Kings Point up near 71, New London running about 69.4 — and that steep west-to-east gradient across the Sound is exactly why the bunker pods have been so thick pushing into the Gut. Peanut bunker schools have been getting pinned against the Plum Gut rip on the last two hours of the incoming, and where the bunker balls up, the blues show up fast and mean. I had a charter Thursday morning working diving birds off Great Gull Island — six- to eight-pound blues on wire, taking Hopkins No-Eql spoons and 2-ounce diamond jigs as fast as we could get them down. No wasted casts. That's the easiest money on the water this week if you don't mind losing a few hooks to the teeth.

Fluke and sea bass have been the quiet story out at the Sluiceway. It's not fast, but it's honest fishing — five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the 60- to 70-foot break where the bottom drops off toward Fishers Island Sound. Sea bass to 17 inches mixed in steady, especially on the last hour of the drift before the tide turned too hard to hold bottom. Nothing that'll fill a cooler by noon, but a solid, repeatable pattern if you're not chasing the blitz.

Now — the question everybody at the dock keeps asking is where the albies are. Short answer: not here yet, but the water's set up for it. We called this too — said the post-new-moon tidal push would be the trigger, and the ingredients are all sitting right in front of us. Bait's dense, the rip current is ripping the way albies like it, and Montauk and Block Island are both close enough that the first fish through either door could show up in Plum Gut or off Little Gull Island inside 72 hours. I've got epoxy jigs rigged and ready — half-ounce Deadly Dick and Albie Snax in bone white — but I haven't thrown one in earnest yet because I haven't seen the nervous water that tells me they're actually in the Gut. When they show, it usually happens fast and all at once, right on the tail of a strong outgoing at Plum Gut when the bait gets squeezed through that funnel.

What I'd tell anybody planning a trip this week: don't build the whole day around the albie hope. Build it around the bass and blues, which are legitimately good right now, and treat any bonito or albie sighting as the bonus. If you're running Valiant Rock or Race Rock, time your drift to hit slack water — check the tide tables for The Race specifically, not just New London harbor, because the timing differs by close to forty minutes and that gap is the difference between a stripe-on-every-drift day and a skunked one. Wire line still rules out there; braid with enough lead can work in the shallower stretches of the Gut, but at Race Rock's depth and current you want the wire down and staying down.

Looking ahead, if this bunker push holds and the tidal flow stays strong through the coming week, I expect the bass bite at Valiant and Race Rock to keep sharpening on those slack windows, and I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first confirmed albie report out of Plum Gut or Fishers Island Sound before the week's out. The water's right. We're just waiting on the fish to catch up to the conditions.
